doc.title: Jane Bunnett interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 25, 2024

chapter: Playing, recording and making a living
title: Making a living as a musician now; teaching in academia
summary: The old tour-record model no longer works, peers teach, and she prefers collaboration and clinics to a teaching position.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Is it a challenge — you’re both practicing musicians and artists. I think I know the answer to this but is it a challenging way to make a living?

Sure is. Really is. Especially right now. You know because the — how do we say it — not the template, but what has worked for so long does not work as well anymore. So what we’ve been conditioned in the last — rehearse a band, go out on tour, come home, make a record, everybody you know goes and does their own thing for a bit, then come back together. Yeah, it’s — with the clubs, you know so many of the clubs, arts presenters, funding cut back for the art presenters received. It’s in a changing environment for artists and so many of my peers are teaching in universities and they’re doing academia to supplement their musical activities. They have to teach. Some people are better teachers than others. And it’s just different because I look at all my musical heroes and the only one I can really think of who taught was Stanley Cowell, the late Stanley Cowell. He was at Rutgers. And he did that because you know I think he found the touring life, you know he had a family and he found the touring life really strenuous. You know he was out on the road with everybody — the Heath Brothers and Rahsaan Roland Kirk and many — but when I think of all the guys, Dewey Redman and Don © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

Pullen and John Hicks and Billy Hart — all these great musicians that I admire, they’ve all just lived off their musical performance. Their playing. Their artistic endeavors. Their creative drive and their expertise in being hired. That’s gone. So I don’t know. It’s just different to really have to, in my case I’m trying to maybe open up a bit more to collaborating with more musicians and so that will allow me to stay in a creative space which is what I really thrive on. I love collaborating, I love throwing ideas out and then getting them thrown back and people adding to make something — enhance it, make it better. I don’t thrive in academia. I still love going out with young people and doing clinics. Like I do a clinic or a workshop but I could not do a full time musical — hold a teaching position. Because it’s just not in my creative spirit.
